sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A phase portrait with trajectories spiraling toward a closed orbit.
sections.body_md:
A limit cycle is an isolated periodic orbit in a nonlinear system. Nearby trajectories either spiral in (stable limit cycle) or spiral out (unstable). Unlike centers in linear systems, limit cycles are isolated: there is no continuous family of periodic orbits at different amplitudes.

Limit cycles require nonlinearity to sustain oscillation. The Van der Pol oscillator has negative damping at small amplitude and positive damping at large amplitude, which drives all trajectories toward a unique orbit. Relay control and saturation can also create limit cycles.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Van der Pol oscillator:
\[
\ddot{x} - \mu(1 - x^2)\dot{x} + x = 0.
\]
For \(\mu > 0\), there is a stable limit cycle.

Hopf bifurcation: a limit cycle is born when a complex eigenvalue pair crosses the imaginary axis.

Describing function: approximate nonlinearity gain \(N(a)\) for input amplitude \(a\). Limit cycle where \(G(j\omega) = -1/N(a)\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A relay controller switches at zero error. The plant is \(G(s) = 1/[s(s+1)]\). The describing function of an ideal relay with amplitude \(M\) is \(N(a) = 4M/(\pi a)\). Intersection of \(-1/N(a)\) with the Nyquist plot of \(G\) gives the limit cycle. If the intersection is at amplitude \(a = 2\) and frequency \(\omega = 1\) rad/s, the relay system oscillates with peak-to-peak swing of 4 and period \(2\pi\) s.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Linear systems cannot have isolated limit cycles; they have either stable equilibria, unstable trajectories, or (marginally) centers with a continuum of closed orbits. The describing function is an approximation; it assumes the nonlinearity sees a sinusoid and higher harmonics are filtered. Multiple limit cycles can coexist in some systems.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Bifurcation theory classifies how limit cycles appear and disappear. Poincaré maps reduce periodic orbit analysis to fixed-point analysis. Lyapunov methods estimate the region of attraction. Describing functions extend to saturation, backlash, and dead zone. Anti-windup and dither mitigate relay chatter.
